transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-06
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 mins
Attendees: Sara Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Liu (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (NovaPay, VP Eng), Tom Reyes (NovaPay, ML Eng), Priya Singh (NovaPay, Platform)

[00:00] Sara Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the weekly sync. Quick check - is this still a 45 minute slot?
[00:06] Aisha Khan: yep, 45 works. We want to focus on the throughput numbers from the last run and tuning suggestions.
[00:15] Marco Liu: Great. I'll share my screen in a sec, but short tl;dr: continuous batching improved tokens/sec across the board but we're seeing p99 latency spikes when concurrency goes above the target. We put together per-shard charts.
[00:30] Tom Reyes: I noticed that too, Marco. When we ramp to 480 concurrent sessions across 4 shards, p50 is fine but p99 jumps to like 1.2s per token which breaks our SLO.
[00:45] Marco Liu: Right, and part of that is queueing behavior. The runtime will batch up to a max batch size if waiting window is long enough, but if concurrency pushes many small requests simultaneously you get fragmentation and uneven GPU utilization.
[01:05] Priya Singh: Can you explain fragmentation? We called this out in doc as 'small batches eating throughput', but not sure of the root.
[01:15] Marco Liu: Sure — think of it as lots of partial batches getting dispatched because the waiting window hit its timeout. So instead of two full 512-batch runs you get several 32-64 partial batches. That increases per-token overhead and inflates tail latency.
[01:30] Sara Patel: How confident are we that increasing waiting window won't blow up latency for interactive users? NovaPay's success criteria still includes 90% of calls under 400ms p95.
[01:42] Marco Liu: Good point. We recommend a hybrid: set a slightly longer window for non-interactive routes (webhooks, batch inference) and keep aggressive windowing for interactive flows. Also use concurrency caps per route so interactive traffic can't starve batching.
[02:00] Aisha Khan: Our main route is a chat-like flow but heavy bursts during payroll windows. We need both low latency and burst handling.
[02:10] Marco Liu: For bursts we suggest enabling burst capacity configuration on Dedicated pools — that gives you spare reserved GPUs for short windows, reduces queue depth, and avoids those p99 spikes. Sara can share pricing.
[02:25] Tom Reyes: In our runs we tried continuous batching with batch-size cap 512 and window 50ms. The profiler shows average batch around 260, but lots of smalls at high concurrency. Any tuning knobs?
[02:40] Marco Liu: Try raising the window to 80-100ms for non-interactive or use adaptive windowing (we have an experimental heuristic that extends window if queue depth expected to reach a full batch). Also use request-level affinity — group similar sequence lengths to avoid wasted padding.
[03:00] Priya Singh: Affinity — we don't currently partition by seq length. How invasive is that?
[03:07] Marco Liu: Low invasiveness — you can set a per-route hint. Runtime will place requests in different batching buckets. It's mostly config, not code changes.
[03:20] Sara Patel: Quick security check — any of these changes affect data residency or logs?
[03:25] Marco Liu: No, it's purely runtime behavior. KV cache and prefix caching keep everything in-memory and respects your VPC/Private deployment controls. We do store metrics and traces in Redwood Console but logs can be turned off or routed to your S3.
[03:40] Aisha Khan: About KV cache — in the last run the KV cache hit was only 12%. Can we improve that?
[03:45] Marco Liu: Two levers: increase keying granularity (use session-level prefix keys) and warm the KV cache with prior steps. Also TTLs — if you have stable prefixes, extend TTL so subsequent requests hit. That will reduce token compute and improve throughput.
[04:05] Tom Reyes: For the benchmarks we saw throughput plateau at ~18k tokens/sec per A100-like shard. Is that expected?
[04:12] Marco Liu: Depends on model and quantization. For your model at 8-bit quant, 18k is plausible. But with improved batching geometry and caching you can push higher. We aim to show per-shard curves so you know the knee of the curve.
[04:30] [00:04:30 visual: Marco shares chart: throughput vs concurrency; spike points marked]
[04:40] Marco Liu: The chart shows throughput rising until ~300 concurrency, then tails flatten and p99 jumps. That's the knee.
[04:50] Aisha Khan: So the ask is: what's the right concurrency target? We don't want to over-provision.
[04:55] Marco Liu: We typically recommend operating slightly left of the knee for predictable p99 — e.g., target 250 concurrency instead of 300. Then use burst capacity to cover rare peaks. Also you can shard more finely and increase GPU packing efficiency.
[05:15] Tom Reyes: Shard more finely — that means more smaller workers? We worried about overhead.
[05:20] Marco Liu: Yes, more workers with lower per-worker concurrency can reduce variance. There is some overhead but with the right kernel selection the runtime handles fragmentation better.
[05:35] Priya Singh: Any config for queueing — like max queue depth or backpressure?
[05:40] Marco Liu: There are settings: max_wait_time_ms, min_batch_size, adaptive_window_enabled, and per-route concurrency_cap. Also queue_length_thresholds that trigger fallback to a cheaper model.
[05:55] Sara Patel: Can you put specific recommended numbers for our traffic?
[06:00] Marco Liu: Based on the trace you shared last week, start with: concurrency_cap=250 for main route, min_batch_size=64, max_batch_size=512, max_wait_time_ms=80 for non-interactive, 30ms for interactive. Enable adaptive_window for batch routes, and set queue_threshold to 120% of capacity to trigger fallback.
[06:20] Aisha Khan: Will that require a code deploy?
[06:24] Marco Liu: No — it's config in Redwood Console or via API. We'll push a sample JSON you can apply.
[06:30] Tom Reyes: About fallbacks — if we trigger fallback to a smaller model during peaks, how does quality degrade? We need to know tradeoffs.
[06:38] Marco Liu: You can set model variants with quality tags. The runtime will attempt same-seq variants first; fallback may reduce context length or use a quantized variant. We'll include expected quality deltas from our eval runs.
[06:55] Priya Singh: Any concerns with SSO or audit when we switch to Dedicated?
[07:00] Sara Patel: Not really — Dedicated keeps your audit logs and integrates with SSO/KMS. We can provide SOC2/ISO docs.
[07:10] Aisha Khan: Good. For the next benchmark we want realistic traffic including payroll bursts, can Redwood run that script?
[07:16] Marco Liu: Yes, if you share the trace we can replay at scale in our test harness and produce the per-shard charts. We'll need payload shapes and sequence length distribution.
[07:26] Tom Reyes: We'll upload those to the shared drive after this call.
[07:30] Sara Patel: Cool. Quick pause — any other blockers from NovaPay?
[07:35] Aisha Khan: Only that we need pricing for burst capacity and an outline of the rollback plan if p99 goes worse.
[07:42] Sara Patel: We'll include a rollback playbook: decrease waiting window, lower concurrency cap, and fall back to hosted variant. Marco will add specifics.
[07:50] Marco Liu: For the rollback steps: step 1 set concurrency_cap lower, step 2 disable adaptive window, step 3 enable fallback to quantized model. I'll document exact API calls.
[08:05] Tom Reyes: In earlier transcripts I saw 'KV cash' spelled wrong sometimes, just a nit — but does observability show which requests hit cache?
[08:12] Marco Liu: Yes — per-request tags show KV_hit true/false in Redwood Console traces. We'll produce a report showing fraction of requests hitting cache by route.
[08:25] Priya Singh: Anything about batching and tokenization differences across sequences? We saw padding variance.
[08:30] Marco Liu: If you can normalize input lengths (truncate or compress) you reduce wasted tokens. We can also cluster by length as mentioned.
[08:42] Aisha Khan: Last question — how long to tune and get us to target?
[08:45] Marco Liu: Two cycles: quick config changes and a replay within 3-5 business days, then an overnight run with tuned settings for final numbers. So about 7-10 days.
[09:00] Sara Patel: Great. Let's recap and assign owners.
[09:05] Aisha Khan: We'll provide trace and payloads by 2027-01-12.
[09:10] Marco Liu: I'll deliver charts (per-shard throughput/latency, batch-size distribution, KV hit report) by 2027-01-10.
[09:15] Sara Patel: I'll send pricing for dedicated pools and burst capacity by 2027-01-08 and attach the rollback playbook.
[09:20] Tom Reyes: We'll review and schedule the run-of-record the week of Jan 18.
[09:25] Sara Patel: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[09:30] Aisha Khan: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
